passed.title: Pass include_header=True to DataFrame.transpose or the column names are lost
passed.trap: By default `DataFrame.transpose` uses `include_header=False`. The original column names are discarded and the new columns get auto-generated names `column_0`, `column_1`, and so on. There is no index to carry the labels as there is in pandas. Pass `include_header=True` (and optionally `header_name=`) to keep the old names as a column, and use `column_names=` to name the value columns.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})

# Default: the names 'a' and 'b' are gone
print(df.transpose())

# Keep the names as a column and name the value columns
print(df.transpose(include_header=True, header_name="field", column_names=["r0", "r1"]))

passed.title: DataFrame.var keeps non-numeric columns as null and uses ddof=1
passed.trap: `DataFrame.var` does not drop non-numeric columns the way pandas `numeric_only=True` would. String columns stay in the result with a `null` value. It also computes the sample variance (`ddof=1`), not numpy's population default (`ddof=0`). Select numeric columns first (for example with `cs.numeric`) and pass `ddof=0` explicitly if you need the population variance.
passed.example:
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "s": ["a", "b", "c"]})

# String column 's' is kept as null; x uses ddof=1 -> 1.0
print(df.var())

# Numeric columns only, population variance -> 0.666667
print(df.select(cs.numeric()).var(ddof=0))

passed.title: DataFrame.vstack returns a new frame unless in_place=True
passed.trap: `DataFrame.vstack` defaults to `in_place=False`. Calling `df1.vstack(df2)` without assigning the result leaves `df1` unchanged, and the stacked rows are silently lost. Either assign the return value or pass `in_place=True`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df1 = pl.DataFrame({"foo": [1, 2], "ham": ["a", "b"]})
df2 = pl.DataFrame({"foo": [3, 4], "ham": ["c", "d"]})

df1.vstack(df2)  # result discarded
print(df1.height)  # still 2

out = df1.vstack(df2)
print(out.height)  # 4

df1.vstack(df2, in_place=True)
print(df1.height)  # 4

passed.title: DataFrame.unstack ordering depends on how, and step does not mean the same thing in each direction
passed.trap: With the default `how="vertical"`, `DataFrame.unstack` fills each new column top to bottom, and `step` is the number of rows in the result. With `how="horizontal"` the values are laid out across the columns instead. In the docstring example, 8 rows with `step=2` produce 4 rows of `x_0`/`x_1`. Using the wrong direction silently assigns values to the wrong cells, so check the output shape and order. If you need grouping by keys, use `DataFrame.pivot` instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]})

v = df.unstack(step=3, how="vertical")
print(v.shape)
print(v)

h = df.unstack(step=3, how="horizontal")
print(h.shape)
print(h)

passed.title: Do not pass the deprecated retries argument to DataFrame writers
passed.trap: The `retries` parameter of `DataFrame.write_csv`, `DataFrame.write_parquet` and `DataFrame.write_ipc` is deprecated since 1.37.1. Omit it from new code. Note also that `DataFrame.write_csv` returns the CSV as a string when `file` is `None`, while `DataFrame.write_parquet` requires a target such as a path or a binary buffer.
passed.example:
import io
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"foo": [1, 2], "bar": ["a", "b"]})

# No retries argument
buf = io.BytesIO()
df.write_parquet(buf)
buf.seek(0)
print(pl.read_parquet(buf).equals(df))

print(repr(df.write_csv()))
